title: HPC Systems Simulation Workbook
text:
Preface
This workbook accompanies the laboratory exercises on High-Performance Computing (HPC) systems at the Faculty of Computer and Information Science, University of Ljubljana.
The exercises use the Structural Simulation Toolkit (SST), a parallel, discrete-event simulation framework developed at Sandia National Laboratories. With SST you build a model of an HPC system from components (processors, caches, memories, network-on-chip and interconnects), wire them together in a Python configuration file and study how design choices affect performance.
Note to Students: These notes are intended solely for educational purposes. They are not a replacement for attending lectures, laboratory sessions, or consulting textbooks, but a complementary resource to support your learning. The material is a work in progress; if something does not work out of the box, report it to your teaching assistant or open an issue.
Acknowledgments:

The material is based on the official SST documentation and the examples distributed with SST-Core and SST-Elements. Many thanks to the SST developers for making them publicly available.

title: 1  Introduction to SST
text:
1.2 Background
SST is a discrete-event simulator. A simulated system is a graph of components (e.g. a core, a cache, a memory controller) connected by links between their ports. Components exchange events over links; every link has a latency. The structure of the system and the component parameters are described in a Python file, which the sst executable loads and runs.
 +-------------+   link (latency)   +-------------+
 | component 0 | port ------- port  | component 1 |
 +-------------+                    +-------------+

title: 1  Introduction to SST
text:
1.4 A first simulation
The file hello_sst.py connects two instances of the simpleElementExample.example0 component, which send each other a fixed number of events.
# Minimal SST configuration: two components exchanging events over one link.
# Uses simpleElementExample.example0 from SST-Elements.
import sst

comp_a = sst.Component("c0", "simpleElementExample.example0")
comp_a.addParams({
    "eventsToSend": 50,
    "eventSize": 32,
})

comp_b = sst.Component("c1", "simpleElementExample.example0")
comp_b.addParams({
    "eventsToSend": 50,
    "eventSize": 32,
})

link = sst.Link("link_c0_c1")
link.connect((comp_a, "port", "1ns"), (comp_b, "port", "1ns"))
Run it:
sst hello_sst.py

1.5 Tasks

Run the simulation and note the simulated time SST reports.
Change the link latency and the number of events. How does the simulated time change?
Enable statistics for both components and inspect the output file.
